articles.title: Apigee Interview Question: What Is the PublishMessage Policy?
articles.excerpt: Preparing for an Apigee Developer interview? The PublishMessage policy is an important topic when discussing asynchronous processing and Google Cloud Pub/Sub integration. The PublishMessage policy all…
articles.body: Preparing for an Apigee Developer interview? The PublishMessage policy is an important topic when discussing asynchronous processing and Google Cloud Pub/Sub integration. The PublishMessage policy allows an Apigee API proxy to publish messages to a Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic, enabling downstream services to process events asynchronously. 1. What Is the PublishMessage Policy? The PublishMessage policy sends a message from an Apigee proxy flow to a Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic. For example, when a payment API receives a successful payment request, Apigee can publish a payment event to Pub/Sub. A downstream service can then process notifications, analytics, or audit events independently. Key benefits: Supports event-driven architectures. Enables asynchronous downstream processing.

articles.title: How to Check Your Own AI Search Visibility Score (By Hand, No Tools)
articles.excerpt: Your page can rank on page one of Google and still never get said out loud by ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity when someone asks the exact question it's supposed to answer. Those are two different syste…
articles.body: Your page can rank on page one of Google and still never get said out loud by ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity when someone asks the exact question it's supposed to answer. Those are two different systems measuring two different things, and almost nobody checks the second one. A search engine indexes a page and returns a list of links. An answer engine does something stranger: it synthesizes a response from whichever sources it judges worth quoting, and then either says your name or doesn't. You can hold a perfectly good ranking and still be invisible to the second system, because ranking well and being citable are not the same skill. Here's the method, and you don't need any tooling to run it. The method Write down the actual questions a buyer would type , not keywords.

articles.title: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED: Rescue Stacks with Force Rollback
articles.excerpt: There is one moment in day-to-day deployments that anyone who has worked with CloudFormation for a while knows: the update fails, the rollback starts, and then the stack just sits there with UPDATE_RO…
articles.body: There is one moment in day-to-day deployments that anyone who has worked with CloudFormation for a while knows: the update fails, the rollback starts, and then the stack just sits there with UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED . No new deployment, no deletion from the pipeline, just a red status and the question of who changed “just a little thing in the console” yesterday. Whether you use CDK, the Serverless Framework or SAM, there is always a CloudFormation stack underneath, so this affects everyone. On October 22, 2026, AWS introduced a new option for exactly this situation: Force Rollback . It gets a stack out of UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED with a single call, even when several resources in nested stacks are stuck. That is convenient.

articles.title: Getting an AI Image to Work in a Website Hero
articles.excerpt: Generate a wide image, put a headline over it, then open the page on your phone. The cup is cropped out. The empty space is gone. The headline now sits over the busiest part of the picture. A 16:9 ima…
articles.body: Generate a wide image, put a headline over it, then open the page on your phone. The cup is cropped out. The empty space is gone. The headline now sits over the busiest part of the picture. A 16:9 image gives you a starting shape. The layout determines how much of it anyone actually sees. That is worth figuring out before spending an afternoon rewriting prompts. Give the image a job in the layout Take a simple landing page: headline on the left, a ceramic coffee cup on the right, one button below the copy. Before generating the image, put the actual headline and button into a rough layout. Use a solid rectangle for the image if necessary. You want to know where the text ends and where the cup can begin. This matters more than it sounds.

articles.title: Listing browser games on a Taiwanese web game hub: what the auto-check looks for
articles.excerpt: I make small free mobile and browser games as a one-person studio in Korea. My numbers keep pointing at Taiwan: in the last 28 days, my internet cafe tycoon got 501 players from Taiwan and 434 from Ko…
articles.body: I make small free mobile and browser games as a one-person studio in Korea. My numbers keep pointing at Taiwan: in the last 28 days, my internet cafe tycoon got 501 players from Taiwan and 434 from Korea. So today I tried 4388.fun, a Taiwanese site that collects free browser games. When I checked it listed about 4.9k games, with 29 new ones in the past 24 hours. There is no review queue. You sign in with Google, paste a game URL, and an automatic check decides on the spot. If the game passes, it is listed right away. You can submit up to 3 games a day. What the check looks at From the submit page: It runs in the browser. No downloads, app store pages, social posts or source-code pages. It uses HTTPS, and the domain is not on Cloudflare's malware and phishing blocklist.

articles.body: A storefront review often starts with screenshots: the homepage, a collection grid, and a product page. Those screens matter, but a customer buys through a sequence. A release needs to be reviewed as that sequence, including the work that happens after checkout. The useful question is not simply whether each page loads. It is whether a person can choose the right item, understand the total, complete checkout, and receive the information the merchant needs to fulfil the order. Build a small test matrix before reviewing the theme Choose representative products rather than testing only the easiest item.

articles.title: 'More missions, more often': NASA is overhauling how it selects science missions
articles.excerpt: NASA is overhauling how it selects and develops science missions, with changes intended to reduce costs, streamline competition and get missions into space faster.
articles.body: NASA is overhauling how it selects and develops science missions, with changes intended to reduce costs, streamline competition and get missions into space faster. The new approach, called Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), was announced on Oct. 21 in an open letter from Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate (SMD), to the NASA science community. The changes, directed by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, could significantly reshape how scientists, universities, NASA centers and commercial companies vie for future missions. "We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long," Fox stated in the letter.

articles.body: Most Android users don’t bother considering browsers beyond Google Chrome , and why would they? It’s quick, it’s stable, and it’ll likely load any web page you throw at it. Why fix something that isn’t broken? However, for power users who aim to rid their phones of big tech influence, there’s a problem: the Google part of that equation. Since it’s Android’s default browser, Chrome is laced with all sorts of Google infusions and limitations. The company has battled against ad-blocking extensions on desktop, while somehow still keeping extension support off of official mobile builds. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.
